q-111798.name: Question 4
q-111798.problem: Which value of $k$ gives precisely one solution to the equation  ${x}^{2}+8=k?$
q-111798.worked_solution:
First, we solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+8 & =k \\ {x}^{2} & =k-8 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & =\sqrt{k-8} \\ |x| & =\sqrt{k-8}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation has only one solution if the right-hand side is equal to zero, and the right-hand side is zero only if the expression underneath the radical is zero. So, we solve for the value of $k$ that makes the expression under the radical equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}k-8 & =0 \\ k & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=8$ will give only one solution to the equation.

q-111797.name: Question 5
q-111797.problem: Which value of $k$ gives precisely one solution to the equation ${t}^{2}+k-8=-2?$
q-111797.worked_solution:
First, we solve for $t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}+k-8 & =-2 \\ {t}^{2} & =-2-k+8 \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{6-k} \\ |t| & =\sqrt{6-k}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation has only one solution if the right-hand side is equal to zero, and the right-hand side is zero only if the expression underneath the radical is zero. So, we solve for the value of $k$ that makes the expression under the radical equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}6-k & =0 \\ k & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=6$ will give only one solution to the equation.

q-23862.name: Question 6
q-23862.problem: Which value of $k$ gives precisely one solution to the equation $(1+3x)^{2}-5=k?$
q-23862.worked_solution:
First, we solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(1+3x)^{2}-5 & =k \\ (1+3x)^{2} & =k+5 \\ \sqrt{(1+3x)^{2}} & =\sqrt{k+5} \\ |1+3x| & =\sqrt{k+5}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation has only one solution if the right-hand side is equal to zero, and the right-hand side is zero only if the expression underneath the radical is zero. So, we solve for the value of $k$ that makes the expression under the radical equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{k+5} & =0 \\ k+5 & =0 \\ k & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=-5$ will give only one solution to the equation.

q-44180.name: Question 7
q-44180.problem: Which value of $k$ gives precisely one solution to the equation ${x}^{2}-1=k?$
q-44180.worked_solution:
First, we solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-1 & =k \\ {x}^{2} & =k+1 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & =\sqrt{k+1} \\ |x| & =\sqrt{k+1}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation has only one solution if the right-hand side is equal to zero, and the right-hand side is zero only if the expression underneath the radical is zero. So, we solve for the value of $k$ that makes the expression under the radical equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}k+1 & =0 \\ k & =-1\end{aligned}

q-111795.name: Question 8
q-111795.problem: Which value of $q$ gives precisely one solution to the equation ${x}^{2}+q+3=7?$
q-111795.worked_solution:
First, we solve for $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+q+3 & =7 \\ {x}^{2} & =7-q-3 \\ {x}^{2} & =4-q \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & =\sqrt{4-q} \\ |x| & =\sqrt{4-q}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation has only one solution if the right-hand side is equal to zero, and the right-hand side is zero only if the expression underneath the radical is zero. So, we solve for the value of $q$ that makes the expression under the radical equal to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}4-q & =0 \\ q & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $q=4$ will give only one solution to the equation.

Let's try and solve using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{2}-4a & =16 \\ {v}^{2} & =16+4a \\ \sqrt{{v}^{2}} & =\sqrt{16+4a} \\ |v| & =\sqrt{16+4a}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation will have no real solutions if the expression under the square root is negative, which gives the following condition:

$$
16+4a<0
$$

We solve this inequality for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}16+4a & <0 \\ 4a & <-16 \\ a & <-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, any value of $a$ that is less than $-4$ will give an equation with no real solutions.

q-23911.name: Question 13
q-23911.problem: Consider the equation $(2x+2)^{2}-1=k.$ For which values of $k$ does this equation have no real solutions?
q-23911.worked_solution:
Let's try and solve using the square root method:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x+2)^{2}-1 & =k \\ (2x+2)^{2} & =k+1 \\ \sqrt{(2x+2)^{2}} & =\sqrt{k+1} \\ |2x+2| & =\sqrt{k+1}\end{aligned}
$$

The equation will have no real solutions if the expression under the square root is negative, which gives the following condition:

$$
k+1<0
$$

We solve this inequality for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k+1 & <0 \\ k & <-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, any value of $a$ that is less than $-1$ will give an equation with no real solutions.
